With nine months of runway remaining at your current burn rate, you must immediately eliminate all feature expansion and pivot toward the second path: ruthless product reduction followed by rapid market testing. Your current software is an unfocused Swiss Army knife. Veterinary clinics do not need thirty minor features; they suffer from extreme administrative fatigue during examinations. 

You should strip away everything except the daily-used medical note-writing tool and the discharge instruction generator. Charge a modest fee, such as one hundred dollars per month, to the clinic currently using it daily, and offer the same terms to the two inactive pilots. This immediately tests willingness to pay, which is the only validation that matters. Do not move to human hospitals. Entering that market requires navigating complex enterprise procurement, intense regulatory oversight, and deeply entrenched legacy vendors with your tiny team and limited cash. 

For the next eight weeks, your engineering efforts should be frozen. Spend week one refining the note-writing workflow based directly on the daily user's feedback to make it frictionless. Weeks two through four require knocking on the doors of twenty local veterinary clinics to sell this single, polished tool. Weeks five through eight will dictate your future: if you secure ten paying clinics, you have a viable micro-SaaS and can cautiously begin fundraising. If you cannot convert local clinics at a low price point, your runway allows you to gracefully wind down or pivot without debt. 

This solution fits your technical background and capital constraints by prioritizing cash generation and product-market fit over vanity metrics and expensive market pivots. The core decision criterion is simple: stop building features for ghosts and verify whether anyone will pay for a single, sharp tool today.
